title: Intake and expenditure are outputs of a regulated system

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Energy intake and energy expenditure are not two independent dials a person sets and then leaves alone. They are outputs of a system that senses body weight, or a signal that tracks it, and pushes back when weight falls. Cut intake, and two things move against the cut.

Expenditure falls by more than the loss of fat and lean mass alone accounts for. After a person sustains a loss of 10% or more of body weight, 24-hour energy expenditure falls by about 20% to 25%, and expenditure ends up about 10% to 15% lower than the change in fat and lean mass alone would predict. The extra fall is the adaptive part: a formerly heavier person now needs roughly 300 to 400 fewer kilocalories (kcal) a day than a person of the same weight and composition who was never heavier. How long this lasts is still disputed.

Appetite rises. Per kilogram lost, eating rises by about 100 kcal a day, more than three times the fall of about 30 kcal a day in expenditure. So the appetite response, not the metabolic one, is the larger of the two.

Both responses run in the direction that returns stored energy toward where it was.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Cut what you eat, and two things start moving against you.

Lose a tenth of your body weight and keep it off, and your daily expenditure drops by about a fifth to a quarter. Some of that drop is exactly what a smaller body should cost to run. The rest is extra: expenditure ends up about 10 to 15% lower than a body of that new size would need.

At the same time your appetite rises. Appetite, not metabolism, does most of the pushing back.

Neither of these is the person’s character failing.

How large the pushback is probably varies between people. The trial behind the appetite estimate reported only a group average.

blocks.alt: Two straight lines from 0 at 0 kg lost. Extra eating reaches about 300 kcal a day at 3 kg lost; the fall in expenditure reaches about 90 kcal a day.
blocks.caption: Per kilogram lost, extra eating rises by about 100 kcal a day and expenditure falls by about 30 kcal a day. For the made-up person 3 kg lighter, that is about 300 against about 90 kcal a day. Both lines are fitted slopes, not measurements of one person.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Take the trial behind the 100 kcal figure, analysed by Polidori and colleagues (2016). It ran for 52 weeks, in 153 people with type 2 diabetes, a condition in which blood glucose runs high. Each took a drug that makes the kidneys pass glucose out in the urine instead of keeping it.

Body weight was measured repeatedly over the year. The researchers worked back, from how weight actually moved, to how much people must have been eating. They found intake climbing as weight fell: close to 100 kcal a day of extra eating for every kilogram already lost.

In the studies Rosenbaum and Leibel review, people holding a loss of a tenth or more of their body weight needed 300 to 400 fewer kcal a day than someone who had always weighed that much. That is the expenditure side of the same loop.

Now compare the two, kilogram for kilogram. Take a made-up person 3 kg lighter than they started, within the several kilograms the trial’s average loss reached. Before any loss, both changes are 0. At 3 kg, extra eating is 3 times 100 kcal, about 300 kcal a day. The fall in expenditure, at about 30 kcal a day per kilogram, is 3 times 30, about 90 kcal a day. Eating has moved more than three times as far.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The 100 kcal per kg figure is a slope fitted to one trial’s group average, in adults with type 2 diabetes losing weight slowly over a year through glucose loss in urine, not from dieting. The trial did not measure expenditure: the 30 kcal per kg comes from other studies, of losses of 10 to 20%. Its authors do not yet know whether the slope holds over a range of weight losses, so the worked case stays within the several kilograms the trial saw.

points.html: “Cut intake and weight keeps falling at the same rate” is incomplete. Treat a plateau in weight loss as the expected output of this loop, not as proof the patient has stopped trying.
A conversation about “slower metabolism” that never mentions rising hunger is describing the smaller half of what the patient is fighting.
A formerly heavier person needs roughly 300 to 400 fewer kcal a day than someone who was always that weight, to hold the same weight. How long that lasts is still disputed.
Do not quote the 100 kcal per kg or the 300-400 kcal figures to a patient as what will happen to them.

blocks.prompt: A colleague says: “This patient’s weight loss has stalled because they’ve stopped sticking to the diet. The arithmetic hasn’t changed, so the only thing that can have changed is their behaviour.” Using this section, say what is wrong with that inference.
blocks.answer: The arithmetic - intake minus expenditure - still holds, but the colleague has assumed both sides are still what they were at the start. As weight falls, expenditure falls with it, so even a fixed intake gives a loss that slows and levels off. Appetite rises at the same time, which makes the prescribed intake harder and harder to hold. A stall therefore cannot tell “stopped trying” apart from either effect. Concluding “stopped sticking to the diet” needs a check on intake, and self-report is a poor check.
